## Evaluation of $\displaystyle I=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{x^{2}}{(x^{2}+4)(x^{4}-1)}\,dx$

### 1. Poles of the integrand

Let $f(z)=\dfrac{z^{2}}{(z^{2}+4)(z^{4}-1)}$. Factor
$$z^{4}-1=(z-1)(z+1)(z^{2}+1),\qquad z^{2}+4=(z-2i)(z+2i).$$
Hence $f$ has **simple** poles at
$$z=1,\;-1\quad(\text{on the real axis}),\qquad z=i,\;2i\quad(\text{upper half-plane}),\qquad z=-i,\;-2i\quad(\text{lower half-plane}).$$

Since the real-axis poles make the ordinary improper integral divergent, the integral is understood as the **Cauchy principal value**, which we compute with the Residue Theorem using a contour that indents the real poles into the upper half-plane.

### 2. Residues

**Real-axis poles.**
$$\operatorname{Res}(f,1)=\frac{z^{2}}{(z^{2}+4)(z+1)(z^{2}+1)}\Big|_{z=1}=\frac{1}{(5)(2)(2)}=\frac{1}{20},$$
$$\operatorname{Res}(f,-1)=\frac{z^{2}}{(z^{2}+4)(z-1)(z^{2}+1)}\Big|_{z=-1}=\frac{1}{(5)(-2)(2)}=-\frac{1}{20}.$$

**Upper half-plane poles.**
$$\operatorname{Res}(f,i)=\frac{z^{2}}{(z^{2}+4)(z-1)(z+1)(z+i)}\Big|_{z=i}=\frac{-1}{(3)(-2)(2i)}=\frac{-1}{-12i}=\frac{-i}{12},$$
$$\operatorname{Res}(f,2i)=\frac{z^{2}}{(z+2i)(z^{4}-1)}\Big|_{z=2i}=\frac{-4}{(4i)(15)}=\frac{-1}{15i}=\frac{i}{15}.$$

### 3. Contour and the residue identity

Take the standard closed contour $\Gamma_R$: the segment $[-R,R]$ on the real axis indented by small upper semicircles of radius $\varepsilon$ around $z=-1$ and $z=1$, closed by the large upper semicircle $C_R$ of radius $R$. For $R>2$ the contour encloses exactly $z=i$ and $z=2i$.

By the Residue Theorem,
$$\oint_{\Gamma_R} f(z)\,dz=2\pi i\bigl(\operatorname{Res}(f,i)+\operatorname{Res}(f,2i)\bigr).$$

The large arc $C_R$ contributes $0$ as $R\to\infty$ since $|f(z)|=O(|z|^{-4})$. Each small indentation semicircle around a real simple pole $a$ is traversed **clockwise**, contributing $-i\pi\,\operatorname{Res}(f,a)$. The remaining real-axis part tends to the principal value $I$. Therefore
$$I\;-\;i\pi\bigl(\operatorname{Res}(f,1)+\operatorname{Res}(f,-1)\bigr)\;=\;2\pi i\bigl(\operatorname{Res}(f,i)+\operatorname{Res}(f,2i)\bigr),$$
i.e.
$$I=2\pi i\sum_{\operatorname{Im}z>0}\operatorname{Res}(f,z)\;+\;i\pi\sum_{\operatorname{Im}z=0}\operatorname{Res}(f,z).$$

### 4. Substitution

Real-axis residue sum:
$$\operatorname{Res}(f,1)+\operatorname{Res}(f,-1)=\frac{1}{20}-\frac{1}{20}=0.$$

Upper half-plane residue sum:
$$\operatorname{Res}(f,i)+\operatorname{Res}(f,2i)=\frac{-i}{12}+\frac{i}{15}=i\!\left(-\frac{1}{12}+\frac{1}{15}\right)=i\!\left(\frac{-5+4}{60}\right)=-\frac{i}{60}.$$

Hence
$$I=2\pi i\!\left(-\frac{i}{60}\right)+i\pi\cdot 0=\frac{2\pi}{60}=\frac{\pi}{30}.$$

### 5. Verification (partial fractions)

Writing $u=x^{2}$,
$$\frac{u}{(u+4)(u-1)(u+1)}=-\frac{4}{15}\frac{1}{u+4}+\frac{1}{10}\frac{1}{u-1}+\frac{1}{6}\frac{1}{u+1}.$$
Thus
$$f(x)=-\frac{4}{15}\frac{1}{x^{2}+4}+\frac{1}{10}\frac{1}{x^{2}-1}+\frac{1}{6}\frac{1}{x^{2}+1}.$$
Using $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dx}{x^{2}+a^{2}}=\frac{\pi}{a}$ and $\displaystyle\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dx}{x^{2}-1}=0$ (the integrand is even with symmetric simple poles, equivalently $\frac{1}{x^{2}-1}=\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\frac{1}{x-1}-\frac{1}{x+1}\bigr)$, a sum of odd functions),
$$I=-\frac{4}{15}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}+\frac{1}{10}\cdot 0+\frac{1}{6}\cdot\pi=-\frac{2\pi}{15}+\frac{\pi}{6}=\pi\!\left(\frac{-4+5}{30}\right)=\frac{\pi}{30}.$$
This agrees with the residue computation.

### Result

$$\boxed{\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{x^{2}}{(x^{2}+4)(x^{4}-1)}\,dx=\frac{\pi}{30}}$$
